newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHENS BROKERS CITE NEW PROBLEM WITH BOURSE BILL.
newsitem.headline: ATHENS BROKERS CITE NEW PROBLEM WITH BOURSE BILL.

text.p: Two Athens bourse members called on Thursday for an urgent meeting of the brokers association to raise concerns about a recent compromise with the government to resolve a bourse settlement crisis.

They said the phrasing of the compromise could provide some parties, who may be linked to a 2.6 billion drachma default at the bourse clearing house this month, with a loophole to dodge legal responsibility.
The brokers want an urgent assembly of the Association of Athens Stock Exchange Members (SMEHA), which groups the 65 brokerages registered to trade on the exchange.

Nuntius Securities and Omega Securities in a letter to SMEHA said they wanted clarification of paragraph three in the bourse bill, which the government fashioned to end the turmoil at the bourse earlier this month.
SMEHA boycotted trade at the bourse for almost four days after the Delta scandal rocked the exchange, saying it wanted the government to ensure better settlement safeguards and to ensure payment.
The moves by Nuntius and Omega are the latest twist of a labourious compromise between SMEHA and the national economy ministry after the Delta scandal.

The offending paragraph states that the exchange's guarantee fund may claim for money it must pay from the broker in default or from any other person who "acted in malice" as a counterparty to trades with the member in default.

Since the party in default is unlikely to have the funds to pay, the paragraph means the guarantee fund can turn to the third parties in the trades for compensation but that the fund must now prove they acted in malice.
Nuntius and Omega are concerned about the phrase "acted in malice", questioning whether malice could be proven in court and noting a definitional vacuum.
Additionally, the letter asks whether SMEHA minutes prove that the association board knew what malice meant when negotiating the draft bill with the national economy ministry.
The two firms also ask what are the likely losses for the guarantee fund which could arise by the failure of the bill to include the phrase "or by negligence" after "acted in malice".

"This appears to be a mistake. It is certain that the SMEHA board could not have intended the inclusion of such a phrase. I am sure that SMEHA could not have accepted this. It must be corrected," Nuntius Securities managing director Alexander Moraitakis told Reuters.

The rationale is that that the phrasing leaves the guarantee fund vulnerable in its claim of funds. Does malice presuppose prior knowledge and intent and if so how could this be proven in a court of law, he said.
A deadlock between SMEHA and the ministry was resolved last week when another contentious phrase was finally removed from an early version of the draft bill.
Delta's default has prompted several audits of SMEHA members and forced authorities to amend legislation to speed up the payment of funds and avert a similar incident from occurring in the future.
